query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature oxidative and corrosive service conditions, the initially metastable solid‐solution Mg-containing lightweight HEA decomposes via thermally activated nucleation and growth of Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds at critical microstructural sites (e.g., grain boundaries). This phase separation alters local diffusion paths and elemental partitioning, thereby disrupting the formation and continuity of the protective oxide scale. Faster or more extensive intermetallic formation will correlate with a degradation of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance compared to the initial state.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state in a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Perform in situ high-temperature characterization (e.g., environmental TEM and/or synchrotron XRD) during controlled aging in oxidizing and corrosive atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant regime involving temperatures above 500 °C (up to ~1100 °C) in air (or controlled oxygen partial pressures) and corrosive exposures (e.g., 3.5% NaCl solution) to simulate in-service degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: The nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds at grain boundaries and other heterogeneities.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated decomposition of the metastable solid solution leads to the localized formation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases. This phase evolution alters elemental distributions—especially of passivating elements (such as Cr or Al, if present as minor additions)—thereby affecting the kinetics and integrity of the protective oxide layer. The altered microstructure, in turn, governs the alloy’s corrosion and high-temperature oxidation response.
generation.predicted_outcome: In situ tests will reveal a time- and temperature-dependent increase in the volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallic phases. Samples exhibiting more rapid or extensive intermetallic formation will display a less continuous or defective oxide scale, correlating with reduced corrosion resistance (evidenced by higher corrosion current densities) and degraded oxidation performance compared to the initial metastable state.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, metastable solid-solution state prior to any significant intermetallic formation.
generation.boundary: Service conditions defined by high-temperature oxidative environments (>500 °C up to ~1100 °C) and corrosive exposures (e.g., salt spray or NaCl solution tests).
generation.uncertainty: The exact rate and extent of intermetallic phase nucleation and their quantitative impact on the protective oxide scale are not well established. Variability in local composition and processing history may also influence the transformation kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing HEA specimens: one maintained in the initial metastable state and another processed under controlled in situ high-temperature oxidation and corrosion conditions. Employ real-time synchrotron XRD or environmental TEM to monitor the onset and growth rate of intermetallic phases, coupled with periodic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and high-temperature oxidation tests.
measurements: Time-resolved phase fraction of intermetallic compounds (via in situ XRD/TEM)
Oxide scale continuity and composition (via SEM/EDS or XPS)
Corrosion current density and polarization resistance (via electrochemical measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ characterization shows no significant nucleation or growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases during high-temperature aging, or if the extent of intermetallic formation does not correlate with a measurable degradation in oxide scale integrity and corrosion/oxidation performance relative to the baseline state, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, CrMnFeCoNi HEA behaviour responding to changes in temperature and environmental factors such as the partial pressure of oxygen has been investigated by in situ XRD at high temperatures up to 1100 °C. In situ thermal observations of materials with the high-temperature XRD provide unique information such as temperature-dependent phase transformations, types of new phase formation, and the start and finish temperatures of competing phases in an alloy system []. In situ HTXRD is instrumental in revealing the real-time of oxide formation as well as the type and temperature at which various kinds of oxide form when metals are exposed to high temperatures in air or in another simulated environment. Our HTXRD analysis provided insight into the thermal stability, phase transitions, and high-temperature oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples, which provides significant guidance in the development of high-performance alloys for demanding applications. The surface and cross-sectional microstructure, elemental distributions, and oxide compositions have been examined to further understand the evolution of the oxides. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are among the promising candidates for the design of structural materials in advanced nuclear energy systems. The effects of Cr, V, Ta, and Ti elements and ball milling on the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of model RHEAs were investigated. The results show that W-rich BCC1 and Ta-rich BCC2 solid solution phases were generated after a long milling duration. After high-temperature sintering, the (Cr, Ta)-rich phase associated with the Laves phase was observed in the Cr-containing model RHEAs. In addition, a high level of Ti, Ta, and V contents promoted the in situ formation of oxide particles in the alloys. Complex TiTa2O7 and Ta2VO6 oxide phases were identified by TEM, which suggests a solid-state reaction of Ti-O, Ta-O, and V-O subjected to high-energy ball milling. The oxide particles are uniformly dispersed in the BCC matrix, which can result in dispersion strengthening and the enhancement of mechanical properties.

frame.system: A magnesium-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (HEA) that is initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state with the propensity to form intermetallic compounds.
frame.goal: To develop a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains the alloy's microstructural evolution—including the transformation pathway and kinetics—and its impact on the retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
frame.limitation: The unresolved and poorly understood transformation pathway and kinetics during aging from a metastable state, particularly how the tendency to form intermetallic compounds governs the evolution of protective properties.
root_cause_cues: tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds
retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance
constraints: Must propose a single testable mechanistic hypothesis
Include an unnamed controlled comparison with a baseline (initial state)
Detail predicted observations relative to the initial microstructure
Define relevant service-regime boundaries (e.g., temperature and corrosive environments)
Reference supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys
Provide a clear falsification result to challenge the hypothesis
frame.regime: Service conditions involving high-temperature oxidative environments and corrosive exposures where the alloy’s protective performance is critical; tests may include controlled thermal cycling and corrosive environment exposures that simulate in-service degradation.
prior_attempts: Prior studies on Mg-containing alloys have noted intermetallic formation but failed to correlate these transformations with the kinetics of microstructural change and performance evolution.
Initial models assumed static metastable states or oversimplified the kinetics, lacking controlled comparisons between as-cast and aged states.
Existing approaches did not fully specify boundary conditions or falsification criteria, resulting in ambiguous interpretations of corrosion and oxidation resistance changes.

decision.trend: Early HEA studies first identified the tendency for intermetallic compounds to emerge as alloy complexity increased (PMC4366518), establishing that configurational entropy alone does not indefinitely stabilize a single solid‐solution phase. Later, research using rapid processing methods such as mechanical alloying showed that non-equilibrium, metastable states could undergo phase evolution into equilibrium mixtures with discernible intermetallic phases (PMC9955146). Most recently, work on lightweight alloys—including Mg-containing systems in complex concentrated alloys (PMC11330973)—demonstrated that processing conditions (e.g., high temperature and pressure) can force a transition toward single-phase stability; however, the precise transformation pathways, kinetics during service aging, and their impact on oxidation/corrosion resistance remain inadequately defined.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved how the metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution state in a Mg-containing lightweight HEA transforms over time into intermetallic-bearing microstructures under service conditions. In particular, linking the kinetics and transformation pathway (including the onset and growth rate of intermetallic compounds) to the retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance—with a proper controlled comparison baseline—has not been demonstrated, and clear falsification criteria are lacking.
decision.lever: Perform real-time, high-temperature in situ characterization (e.g., environmental TEM or synchrotron XRD) on the Mg-containing HEA under controlled oxidative and corrosive atmospheres, while systematically varying aging time and temperature to capture the nucleation and growth of intermetallic phases.
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the trend moving from static post-mortem analyses to dynamic, in situ tracking of microstructural evolution. It enables a controlled comparison between the initial metastable state and the aged state, defines service-regime boundaries via temperature and environmental control, and provides a clear falsification criterion (i.e., failure to observe the predicted intermetallic nucleation kinetics and associated changes in corrosion/oxidation behavior would invalidate the mechanistic hypothesis).
